name: INA260AIPWR
title: Digital current, voltage and power monitor with integrated 2 mΩ precision shunt, I2C/SMBus
summary: The INA260 measures the current through its own built-in 2 mΩ Kelvin shunt, the voltage on a bus of 0 V to 36 V, and multiplies the two to give power, reporting all three over an I2C or SMBus-compatible interface in amperes, volts and watts with fixed LSBs. Current may flow either way and the shunt may sit on the high or low side; the bus range does not depend on the 2.7 V to 5.5 V supply. An open-drain ALERT output trips on one programmable limit or on conversion ready, and two address pins give 16 bus addresses. It comes in a 16-pin TSSOP rated for 15 A continuous to 85 °C.
key_figures: 2 mΩ (4.5 mΩ total IN+ to IN–)

tables.title: Mask/Enable register (06h) fields
rows: Over current limit: ALERT asserts when a current result is above the Alert Limit value.
Under current limit: ALERT asserts when a current result is below the Alert Limit value.
Bus voltage over-voltage: ALERT asserts when a bus voltage result is above the limit.
Bus voltage under-voltage: ALERT asserts when a bus voltage result is below the limit.
Power over-limit: ALERT asserts when the power figure computed after a bus voltage conversion is above the limit.
Conversion ready: ALERT asserts when CVRF (bit 3) sets.
Alert function flag: tells whether the alert function caused an alert. Latched: cleared by reading this register. Transparent: cleared by the next conversion with no alert.
Conversion ready flag: sets when conversions, averaging and multiplication finish. Cleared by a write to the Configuration Register (other than one selecting power-down) or a read of this register.
Math overflow flag: 1 when an arithmetic result overflowed; power may have gone beyond the 419.43 W limit of the register.
Alert polarity: 1 = inverted (active-high open collector); 0 = normal (active-low open collector), the default.
Alert latch enable: 1 = latched, ALERT and AFF hold after a fault until this register is read; 0 = transparent, both return to idle once the fault clears (default).

circuits.title: High-side current, voltage and power monitor
circuits.description: The INA260's internal shunt is put in series with the positive rail: the 0 V to 36 V supply enters IN+ and leaves IN- to the load, whose return is ground. VBUS is tied to the supply side so the bus voltage is read there. VS is the 2.7 V to 5.5 V device supply with C1, 0.1 µF, to ground. SDA, SCL and the open-drain ALERT each have a pull-up to VS and go out to the host; A0 and A1 come out to be strapped for the bus address.
notes: IN+ stands for pins 1 to 3, IN- for pins 14 to 16 and GND for pins 6 and 11.

operation.text: The shunt is a four-wire Kelvin resistor whose sense connections are made inside the package, which removes most of the parasitic impedance a discrete low-value shunt brings; the part is calibrated so the shunt and the sense amplifier match. Of the roughly 4.5 mΩ between IN+ and IN-, 2 mΩ is the controlled sense element the ADC reads; heating, and so the current limit, follows the full 4.5 mΩ. The shunt is reachable at the pins but is not meant for use on its own. The current limit keeps the resistor and package undamaged and the die at or below 150 °C.

With no air flow, 1 oz copper input planes and up to 85 °C ambient, the part carries 15 A continuously. Above 85 °C the rating falls, reaching 10 A at 125 °C. With air flow and 2 oz copper planes it carries 15 A across –40 °C to 125 °C. Ambient, air flow and board copper decide how well heat leaves the package.
Short excursions beyond 15 A do not harm the shunt or amplifier, within the overload-current-versus-time curve; at or above that curve the part may be damaged or its readings left permanently wrong.

The monitored bus may be 0 V to 36 V whatever the 2.7 V to 5.5 V supply is, and either may be present without the other, so no power sequencing is needed. The inputs stand the full 0 V to 36 V with or without VS applied. No more than 36 V may be applied to the inputs even though the bus register spans 40.96 V.

With MODE = 111 (the default) the ADC alternates a shunt reading and a bus reading. After each shunt reading the current is worked out, and from it the power; each result is added into an accumulator until the set number of averages is reached, then current, bus voltage and power are written to their output registers together. Those registers hold their values until the next complete set replaces them, and reading them does not disturb a conversion. Other MODE codes convert only current or only bus voltage. Current and power calculations run in the background and add nothing to the conversion time.
Writing MODE 001, 010 or 011 starts one single-shot set of conversions. Each further single shot needs another write to the Configuration Register, even with the same mode.
Power-down lowers the supply current and stops current into the inputs. Registers can still be read and written. The part stays down until an active mode is written, and takes 40 µs to recover fully.

The last results can be read at any time. CVRF in the Mask/Enable Register sets once all conversions, averaging and multiplication are done, to pace single-shot use. It clears on any Configuration Register write except one selecting power-down, and on a read of the Mask/Enable Register.
Reading it has no effect on settings or on a conversion. A write halts any running conversion until it completes, then a new conversion begins with the new settings.

ALERT is open drain and watches one of five functions chosen in the Mask/Enable Register against the single Alert Limit Register: over current (OCL), under current (UCL), bus over-voltage (BOL), bus under-voltage (BUL) or power over-limit (POL). If more than one is set, the highest bit wins. Current limits are compared after each current conversion; bus and power limits after each bus voltage conversion. Conversion ready may also drive ALERT alongside one function; then reading AFF (bit 4) and CVRF (bit 3) tells which caused it. The Alert Limit Register takes the format of the register it is compared with. An unused ALERT may be left open.

AFF sets whenever the watched value passes the limit, and ALERT follows with the polarity set by APOL (default active low). With the latch enabled, AFF and ALERT stay set until a Configuration Register write or a Mask/Enable Register read; transparent, they release once the condition is gone.

With a 5.5 V bus over-voltage threshold and averaging 1, ALERT asserted 140 µs to 280 µs after the bus crossed the limit at tCT = 140 µs, and 1.1 ms to 2.2 ms at tCT = 1.1 ms: one to two conversions for a fault just past the limit, depending on where in the ADC cycle it arrives. A fault far beyond the limit can trip in under one conversion, since fewer samples are needed to pull the average past it. ALERT needs a pull-up to the VS voltage.

Conversion times run from 140 µs to 8.244 ms and may differ for current and bus voltage. Longer conversions and more averages lower noise; the most accurate results come from the longest times and most averages the system's update rate allows. Example: 588 µs for both with 4 averages updates about every 4.7 ms; 4.156 ms for current, 588 µs for bus voltage with 1 average also updates about every 4.7 ms, useful when the bus is steady.
Registers are volatile: any non-default setting has to be written again after every power-up.

The part is a slave only, on I2C or SMBus, through open-drain SDA and SCL, both needing external pull-ups. SCL is an input only and the part never stretches the clock. SDA and SCL have spike-suppression filters and Schmitt triggers. Clock rates of 1 kHz to 400 kHz (fast mode) and up to 2.94 MHz (high-speed mode) are supported, and data go most significant byte first. A 28 ms timeout resets the interface if SCL is held low, so the bus cannot lock up. A0 and A1 are sampled on every transaction, each tied to GND, VS, SDA or SCL, giving 16 addresses from 1000000 to 1001111.

Every write starts with the slave address (R/W low) and then the register pointer byte; for a register write two data bytes follow, MSB first, each acknowledged by the part. A read returns the register last pointed to: to change it, write the address and pointer only, then send a start and the address with R/W high, and the part sends MSB then LSB. The master ends with a not-acknowledge or a start or stop. The pointer stays put, so repeated reads of one register need no new pointer.

The master sends the HS master code 00001XXX at 400 kHz or less after a start; the part does not acknowledge it but switches its input deglitch filters for high speed. After a repeated start, transfers up to 2.94 MHz follow the normal protocol. Repeated starts hold HS operation; a stop condition returns the filters to fast/standard mode.

With alerts latched, the part answers the SMBus Alert Response address 0001 100 sent with R/W high by acknowledging and giving its own address. If several devices answer, arbitration lets the lowest address through first; the others keep holding the alert line low until served. The part lets go of the alert line once it has answered, but its internal flags stay set until the host clears them.

A 0.1 µF bypass capacitor is typical, placed as close as possible to VS and GND. Noisy or high-impedance supplies may need more decoupling. The device can run from 5 V while monitoring a bus as high as 36 V.

Bring the current straight into and out of the shunt pins so it spreads evenly through the package, with traces sized for the current. Wide copper pours from the pins to the connectors lower resistance and draw heat away. Bypass capacitors go next to their pins on a thick trace without vias; if the ground does not join on the top layer, use several vias to the capacitor grounds. VBUS connects to the supply rail. The pull-ups on ALERT, SDA and SCL are not critical to placement. Keeping SDA and SCL apart, with ground between layers or shielding, reduces coupling that could be mistaken for start or stop conditions.
